title: Capstone Showcase, Review, and Launch
summary: The final day is about consolidation and launch - turning 45 days of learning, a real capstone, and a portfolio into concrete action that starts your automation career. You begin with a review across the whole journey: you now understand automation f
content:
# Capstone Showcase, Review, and Launch ##### Forty-five days ago On Day 1 you were asked to write down five repetitive tasks and identify their triggers and actions. That was the whole exercise. No tools, no code, just noticing that ordinary work has a shape. Today you have a deployed, monitored, documented multi-system automation with a database, an AI step and measured business impact. Somewhere in between, the thing that changed was not just knowledge — it was how you see problems. You now look at a manual process and automatically decompose it into events, data, decisions, failure modes and a measurable outcome. That perception is the actual asset. Tools will change; Zapier's interface will be redesigned, n8n will ship features that make half of what you learned easier, and whatever agent framework leads today will be superseded. The decomposition instinct will still be there. Today is not about learning something new. It is about **consolidating** what you have and **launching** — turning 45 days of work into applications sent, messages written, and a public profile that says what you can do. ##### A final review of the ground you covered Take ten minutes and genuinely look at the arc, because it is easy to lose sight of: **Foundations (1–5).** What automation engineering is, triggers and actions, APIs and HTTP, JSON, webhooks. The mental model everything else sits on. **Platforms (6–12).** Zapier fundamentals and advanced logic, Make's canvas with routers, iterators and aggregators, n8n with expressions, HTTP requests and code — then the judgment to choose between them. **Integration and data (13–19).** Authentication and OAuth, Google Workspace, communication platforms, CRMs and deduplication, transformation and time zones, error handling and idempotency, scheduling and cron. **Code and depth (20–25).** Python fundamentals, requests and files and secrets, browser automation, web scraping and its ethics, RPA and Power Automate, databases and SQL. **AI and engineering practice (26–32).** LLMs in workflows, agents with tools and RAG, Git and GitHub, testing and debugging, security and privacy, monitoring and observability, Docker and deployment. **Applied and professional (33–45).** Document automation, e-commerce and marketing, design patterns, multi-system orchestration, the three-part capstone, freelancing and delivery, the wider ecosystem, portfolio, interviews, and career paths. Now do the honest self-assessment. Rate yourself 1–5 on each block. Your **weakest area is your next learning target**, and your **strongest is what you lead with** in applications. Both pieces of information are useful; neither is a judgment. ##### Polishing the capstone demo Your demo video is the highest-leverage artefact you own. It gets watched when a résumé gets skimmed. Structure it tightly: ```text 0:00-0:30 THE PROBLEM "A logistics team spent 16.5 hours a month re-keying supplier confirmations, with about three errors a month reaching customers." Show the manual process if you can — a screen of the old spreadsheet. 0:30-2:30 THE AUTOMATION, RUNNING Trigger it live. Show real data flowing. Narrate what is happening. Show the exception path too — not just the happy path. 2:30-3:30 ARCHITECTURE AND ONE DECISION The diagram, then one interesting trade-off explained: "I used LLM extraction rather than regex because 14 suppliers meant 14 formats, and template changes would break regex." 3:30-4:00 THE IMPACT The before/after table. Real numbers, measured over a real period. ``` Recording notes that matter: rehearse once so you are not discovering your own UI on camera, keep it under five minutes, use real data (sanitized), and show something failing gracefully — demonstrating that you handle errors is more impressive than demonstrating that things work. Loom, OBS or even a phone recording of your screen is fine; production value is not the point. ##### Personal brand: LinkedIn, GitHub, outreach **LinkedIn** is where recruiters look. Make each element work: - **Headline** — "Automation Engineer | n8n, Make, Zapier, Python, AI Workflows | I automate business processes and measure the result." Not "Aspiring automation enthusiast." Drop "aspiring"; you have shipped a production automation. - **About** — tell one project's story in three short paragraphs: the problem, what you built, the measured result. End with what you are looking for. - **Featured** — pin your portfolio, your capstone case study and your demo video. - **Experience** — describe projects as impact, not activity: *"Built and deployed an n8n + PostgreSQL + LLM pipeline that cut order confirmation time 92%."* - **Activity** — post your capstone write-up. Then post something useful monthly. This is the cheapest, highest-return marketing available to you. **GitHub** should look alive: a profile README introducing you and linking three projects, each repository with a real README, workflow exports committed, and recent commit activity. A hiring manager who opens your GitHub and finds structured, documented work has learned more than any interview round could tell them in the same two minutes. **Outreach** works when it is specific. A template that gets replies: ```text Subject: Automating your [specific process] — quick idea Hi [Name], I noticed [specific, true observation about their business — you posted about handling orders manually / your careers page mentions ops workload]. I recently built an automation for a [similar business] that cut supplier confirmation processing from 22 minutes to under 2, eliminating manual re-keying errors entirely. Short demo here: [link] If something similar would be useful for [their process], I'd be glad to map it out in 20 minutes at no cost — you'd get a clear plan either way. Ananya [portfolio link] ``` Specific observation, relevant proof with a number, low-commitment ask. Send ten of these and you will get replies; the generic version sent to a hundred gets none. ##### Applying and launching ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Portfolio + demo ready] --> B[Profiles updated
LinkedIn · GitHub] B --> C[Target list
20 roles + 20 businesses] C --> D[Apply / outreach
5 per week, tailored] D --> E[Track responses
in a sheet] E --> F[Interview + iterate
on feedback] F --> G[Offer / first client] E -.no response in 2 weeks.-> H[Follow up once] H --> E ``` Practical mechanics: - **Build a target list** — 20 roles and 20 local businesses whose process you could plausibly automate. - **Tailor every application.** Link the *one* most relevant case study, not the whole portfolio. Reference something specific about the company. - **Track everything** in a sheet: date, company, contact, what you sent, response, follow-up date. Automate the reminder — you have the skills, and it is a nicely appropriate final project. - **Follow up once** after two weeks. A polite follow-up converts a surprising share of silences. - **Expect a low response rate.** Ten applications to one interview is normal. This is a volume-plus-quality process, not a lottery you should read personally. - **Apply slightly above your level.** Postings list wishes, not requirements. If you match 60–70%, apply. - **Ask for feedback** after every rejection. Some will answer, and those answers are worth more than another course. ##### Committing to a cadence The learning does not stop today, but motivation is unreliable — so replace it with a schedule you can sustain when you are tired: ```text Daily 30-45 min reading, docs, or a course module Weekly 3-4 h build something (project, template, experiment) Weekly 1 h write publicly about what you built Monthly 2 h try one new tool; update portfolio and tools journal Quarterly 1 h review the growth plan; reassess the target Yearly one substantial project that stretches you ``` Two rules make it stick. **Ship something publicly every month** — a post, a template, a repository — because a visible cadence compounds into reputation. And **keep an impact log**: one line per thing you build, with the outcome. In a year it becomes your résumé, your review material, and your interview stories, all written while the details were fresh. ##### Common pitfalls at this stage - **Waiting until you feel ready.** You will not. Apply now; readiness arrives through interviewing. - **Perfectionism on the portfolio** while sending zero applications. - **Generic mass applications** with no tailoring. - **Stopping after ten rejections.** The variance is high; the process works over dozens. - **Not asking for feedback.** - **Letting the portfolio go stale** after landing something — keep shipping. - **Underselling yourself.** You have deployed a monitored, documented production automation with measured impact. Many working professionals have not. - **Learning in private.** Public work compounds; private work does not. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task is deliberately action-forcing: do a **full recorded dry-run presentation** of your capstone, **update LinkedIn and GitHub** to present you as an automation engineer with linked projects, and **draft your first three applications or outreach messages**. Draft is the operative word — the mini project is where you send them. The mini project: assemble and **launch the complete package** — polished portfolio and demo, updated profiles, a shortlist of target roles and clients, and **actually send** the first applications or outreach messages, logging responses for follow-up. Sending is the entire point. A perfect portfolio nobody has seen is a private hobby. For the assignment, write your **one-page reflection**: what you learned across the 45 days, your strongest and weakest areas, and a concrete **30-day action plan** for landing your first role or client. Make the plan specific and dated — "week 1: finish case study three and send five applications; week 2: five more plus three local business outreach; week 3: mock interview and iterate on feedback; week 4: review response rate and adjust the targeting." Vague plans produce vague outcomes. ##### Key takeaways - The durable asset from these 45 days is the instinct to decompose any manual process into events, data, decisions, failure modes and a measurable outcome. - Review the whole arc honestly: your weakest block is your next learning target, your strongest is what you lead with. - Your demo video and case studies do the persuading — problem, live run including an exception, one interesting decision, measured impact. - Present yourself as what you now are: update LinkedIn and GitHub, then apply and reach out with specific, evidence-backed, tailored messages. - Replace motivation with cadence — build weekly, publish monthly, keep an impact log — and start sending applications before you feel ready, because readiness comes from the process.
